findings.trigger: Two presses that both call add_user_cooldown() at nearly the same moment (one via the Waitress web thread - e.g. a panel-triggered action - and one via the bot's event loop thread, which the comment at lines 134-138 says both use this same service instance): one thread runs the list comprehension `old_keys = [... for key, timestamp in self._user_cooldowns.items() ...]` at line 471 while the other thread does `self._user_cooldowns[cooldown_key] = current_time` at line 463, adding a new key. self._user_cooldowns has no lock (only self._window_lock guards self._minute_windows, per the comment at line 137). CPython raises 'RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration' when a dict is resized while another thread iterates it - this can raise out of add_user_cooldown, which runs right after a button/command was already accepted, so a container action already executed while the follow-up bookkeeping call raises.
findings.suggestion: Guard all reads/writes of self._user_cooldowns (in is_on_cooldown, get_remaining_cooldown, add_user_cooldown) with self._window_lock (or a second dedicated lock), the same way self._minute_windows already is.
findings.unsure_why: The race and the unguarded dict are real and self-documented in the code comment. What I cannot see from this section alone is how often the two threads actually call this concurrently in practice, and whether the caller outside this file (docker_control.py / main_routes.py) catches a stray RuntimeError from this call, which would change how visible the failure actually is to the user.

findings.trigger: SpamProtectionConfig.from_dict (line 37-48) validates nothing in command_cooldowns/button_cooldowns - it just does `dict(data.get('command_cooldowns', {}))` (line 41) and the same for buttons. Only the two global per-minute numbers get the recovery path via _without_bad_numbers (line 479). The code comment at lines 64-66 says that before 2026-09-26 bad values ('abc', -5, 10**9, true) could already have been written into a per-button/per-command cooldown in channels_config.json by the panel. If such a legacy non-numeric value is still sitting in an existing installation's file, get_command_cooldown/get_button_cooldown hand it back unchanged, and is_on_cooldown's `(current_time - last_used) < self._cooldown_for(action_type, is_command)` at line 418 (also reached from get_remaining_cooldown at line 439) compares a float to that value - a TypeError for a non-numeric value, raised on every press of that button/command from then on.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same kind of per-key numeric sanitisation used in _without_bad_numbers() to command_cooldowns/button_cooldowns as well, so a bad legacy value is dropped (falls back to default) instead of reaching the comparison.
findings.unsure_why: I cannot see whether some other code (a migration, or the fact that channels_config.json is always rewritten by save_config()'s to_dict()) already scrubs old bad values before this could ever be hit on an upgraded installation; the panel-side problems_in() only blocks a NEW bad save, not an old one already on disk.

findings.trigger: _pre_render_shadow_image() writes the finished cache file directly to its final name (`silhouette_img.save(shadow_path, ...)` at line 230-236), and _pre_render_unlocked_image() does the same with `open(unlocked_path, 'wb'); f.write(animation_bytes)` at lines 276-277 - neither goes through a temp-file+rename. If the process is killed/crashes mid-write (or, since nothing locks the cache directory, two overlapping calls for the same level write the same filename at once), a partial/corrupt .webp is left under the final name. _is_pre_rendering_needed() only checks `cache_path.exists()` (line 154) - a half-written file counts as 'already cached' - so it is never regenerated, and get_mech_display_image() (line 306) reads it, returns success=True with the corrupt bytes, and that broken image is what Discord ends up trying to render, indefinitely, until someone calls clear_cache() or passes force_regenerate.
findings.suggestion: Write to a temp file in the same directory and os.replace() it onto the final path, the way utils/atomic_io.py already does elsewhere in this codebase, so a partial write never appears under the final cache filename.

findings.trigger: If no control channel is configured when a new version first starts, send_update_notification() (line 274-277) calls self.mark_notification_shown() with no channel_ids, which only sets status['last_notified_version'] (line 225) and never touches status['channels_notified'] for this version. If the operator later adds a control channel, should_show_update_notification() (line 191-205) now sees last_notified_version == current_version, falls to line 205, and `self.current_version in status.get('channels_notified', {})` is False (the key was never created) - so the function returns False and the newly-added control channel never receives that version's update notice, even though it has genuinely never seen it.
findings.suggestion: Either treat a missing channels_notified[version] key the same as an empty list needing channels_still_to_tell() to run (so a later-added control channel can still be told), or explicitly document this as an accepted gap the way B12/B13 document other exceptions to a guarantee.
findings.unsure_why: The comment at lines 202-204 ('A mark without a list is from before that list existed, or from a setup without control channels') reads as if this exact case was considered and accepted rather than overlooked, but it is not recorded under 'Deliberate decisions' in SPEC.md, so I cannot tell whether it is an accepted trade-off or a residual gap.

findings.trigger: _set() (called from record_result at lines 234/249 and from note_query_failure at line 278) persists via `_atomic_update(lambda s: s.update({name: entry}), self._path)` at line 329, where `entry` is a brand-new dict built at lines 314-323 that has no 'testing' key at all. The module doc for _atomic_update says writers 'never overwrite verdicts owned by the other', but that promise is only kept at the per-container-name granularity, not per-field: if a manual re-test is in progress for a container (module-level set_testing() at line 151 set entry['testing']=True in the shared file, additively, preserving the other fields) and, before record_manual_success() clears it, the same container also goes through a normal record_result()/note_query_failure() call (e.g. the automatic prober touching a still-probing or demoted/silent container), _set()'s full-entry replace drops the 'testing' key entirely - the panel's re-test spinner (driven by that flag, per the module docstring at line 151-152) can stop appearing to be in progress before the actual re-test call it was tracking has reported anything.
findings.suggestion: Have _set() preserve an existing 'testing' key from the current entry (e.g. read it from state.get(name) inside the mutate closure) instead of building a wholly new dict that always omits it.
findings.unsure_why: I cannot see the web-panel code that reads the 'testing' key to drive the spinner, so I cannot confirm how a dropped flag actually shows up in the UI, nor how often a manual re-test and an automatic probe would really overlap on the same container in practice.

notes: This section (4 files) is already unusually heavily reviewed - most functions carry inline comments citing prior review passes ('review C29', 'C64', 'C65', 'C66', 'final check before v3.1.0') that fixed real bugs, and the remaining logic (probe lifecycle in game_query_support_service.py, the cooldown/window arithmetic in spam_protection_service.py, the per-channel notification bookkeeping in update_notifier.py) checked out consistent with its own doc comments. F3's two call sites (_pre_render_shadow_image, _pre_render_unlocked_image) are private helpers not listed individually in PLAN.txt, so I attached the finding to the two public methods that create/serve the affected cache files (pre_render_all_displays, get_mech_display_image) instead. None of F1-F5 touch money, container actions, or permissions (Z1-Z6, Z9 in SPEC.md are unaffected by anything in this section); they are all either concurrency/robustness gaps or a UI-visibility edge case.
